newsitem.title: EGYPT: Mubarak says Egyptian Copts equal to Moslems.
newsitem.headline: Mubarak says Egyptian Copts equal to Moslems.

text.p: Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak on Wednesday said Christian Copts in Egypt had the same rights and duties as the country's Moslem population.

Mubarak was responding to comments made by the spiritual leader of the Moslem Brotherhood earlier this month in which he said Copts should not hold leading positions in the armed forces in case Egypt had to fight a Christian country.
In his annual speech to mark Labour Day, Mubarak condemned what he called attempts by outside forces to export sectarian strife to Egypt.
He did not say who was behind the attempt, but linked the latest attack on Egypt's Coptic Christians to an anti-government campaign launched by Moslem militants in 1992.
Militants have targeted Christians along with senior officials, policemen and occasionally tourists in their attempt to overthrow the government and set up a strict Islamist state.
Egyptian officials maintain they have put a brake on the activity of the militants, who they say were funded from abroad.

"They tried unsuccessfully to export sectarian strife to a nation that prides itself on its tolerance and its national unity and they are trying again after their criminal plans have failed," Mubarak said in the speech, which was broadcast on state television.

"But Egyptians, Copts and Moslems, know the vileness of this goal and the dimensions of the conspiracy. Egypt's Copts are a fundamental part of its national fabric. They are honourable citizens who have the same rights as we (Moslems) do and share our duties," he said to applause.
The head of Egypt's Coptic church Pope Shenouda sat in the front row of the auditorium, alongside ministers and officials.
The comments by the Brotherhood's Mostafa Mashour came on the heels of two bloody Moslem militant attacks in which the majority of victims were Christians.

Suspected militants massacred 10 young Christians in a church in southern Egypt in February and shot dead 13 people in a bloody rampage in a predominantly Christian hamlet also in the south a month later.
The government has portrayed the outlawed and influential Brotherhood as a front for the violent militant groups.
But the organisation, Egypt's largest political Islamic group, denies the charge, saying it wants to change Egypt into a strict Islamic state through legal means such as elections.
"I urge our brothers who give media interviews to take into account Egyptian values and principles and to fully know that Moslems and Copts all work under one flag, the Egyptian flag," Mubarak said.

"We have always lived together and we will not change or be divided. I have my own faith and you have yours but we are all Egyptians. Everyone is free. Religion is for God and the nation is for all. We will always abide by this principle," he added.

Official figures estimate Christians account for 10 percent of Egypt's 60 million people, but Christians give a slightly higher figure. Copts also complain that they have never held top ministerial posts and are sometimes discriminated against in the workplace.
